newsitem.title: USA: Stocks clobbered as bond market falls.
newsitem.headline: Stocks clobbered as bond market falls.

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average tumbled Wednesday as investors were rattled by weakness in the bond market that pushed long-term interest rates higher.
The index of 30 blue-chip stocks fell 139.67 points, or 1.93 percent, to close at 7,085.65, backing off from Tuesday's record finish of 7,225.32.

It was the Dow's steepest plunge since April 11 and erased most of the 154 points it had gained during back-to-back record-setting sessions in the two prior days, including a 143-point rise on Monday.
In the broader market, declining issues outnumbered advances 1,657 to 845 on active volume of 497 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
With the majority of corporate earnings already reported for the quarter, investors had little choice but to focus on the bond market.
"When there are no earnings to move the market, the stock market and bond market move in tandem," said Robert Froehlich, chief investment strategist at Kemper Funds.

The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond fell 29/32 point, or $9.06 per $1,000 face value, raising its yield to 6.96 percent from 6.89 percent on Tuesday after a disappointing auction of 10-year Treasury notes.
Financial stocks bore the brunt of the selling. J.P. Morgan & Co. dropped 3-1/2 to 101-3/8, the largest fall among the Dow components.
The Dow's other financial components also slumped. American Express Co. lost 2-3/8 to 66 and Travelers Group Inc. fell 2-1/2 to 54-3/8.
With attention again focused on interest rates, analysts said the market's next turn could quickly put the market's recent fierce rebound to the test.

"Certainly if rates keep rising and volatility keeps going along the way it has, that's going to give investors cause to pause and think about what it is they're doing," said Charles White, managing director at Avatar Associates.
While financial stocks were battered, few sectors were left out of the market's widespead sell-off. Technology stocks ended lower, as did small-name stocks.

One financial stock that bucked the trend was Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc., which jumped 3-7/8 to 38 on heavy volume of more than 7 million shares. Traders cited a wave of rumours linking a number of major banks to a possible acquisition of the Wall Street firm.
Lehman declined to comment on the rumours.
Fluor Corp. fell 8-1/4 to 47-3/4 in NYSE activity after warning late Tuesday that it expected to report a fiscal second quarter loss of $70 million.
Transitional Hospitals Corp. gained 1-1/8 to 15-1/2 after Vencor Inc. launched a $16-per-share, $639 million tender offer for all the company's shares.
Vencor's bid topped a competing $14.55-per-share offer for Transitional from privately-held Select Medical Corp. Vencor shares fell 3-1/8 to 39-7/8.

Cisco topped the Nasdaq most actives list, rising 1 to 58-3/4, even though it posted quarterly results that were short of Wall Street's expectations. 3Com Corp. gained 1-3/8 to 37-1/8. U.S. Robotics Corp., which announced a merger with 3Com in February, rose 2-1/2 to 63-7/8.
Premier Research Worldwide Ltd. sank 1-5/8 to 7 after saying its revenues and earnings for the second quarter and 1997 overall would fall short of analysts' estimates.
The Nasdaq Composite index lost 5.39 points to 1,322.91.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 12.14 points to 815.62. The American Stock Exchange index slipped 0.01 to 570.50.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 5.82 to 424.95. The average share was down 58 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,706.981 down 93.28x or 1.20 percent.
